thesis: Briggs's lab has already gotten microbes to pull rare earths out of coal in the lab and then hit the scale-up wall, so the AI in this $6M plan isn't a miner, it's a fast no: a model meant to call a failing reactor and a dead-end feedstock early instead of after months or years, which helps Alaska win only if that shortcut survives the jump from lab to plant.
falsifiability: False if, by the award's end in August 2030 (c27), the model's early calls don't shorten the work: reactors it watched fail as often as before (c16, c17), feedstocks it would have ruled out turn out to work, or recovery still drops from lab to larger reactors the way a DOE-funded coal pilot's did (c23). Also false today if the sources gave the AI the extraction job; they don't, the microbes do it (c8, c14).
supporting_facts: The problem is concentration, not scarcity. Per Briggs the rare earths are not rare (c2), the hard part is concentrating them from very dilute sources (c3), and today's route can take strong acids, high temperatures, solvents and 200 steps (c5). He hopes for four or five (c12).

The lab part already worked once and stopped there. His lab has used microbes to pull rare earths from coal before (c32), but the process hasn't been scaled up to be commercially viable (c33). Microbes already recover copper and gold at industrial scale (c13), so biology can scale.

The AI is aimed at time and stability. A deep-learning model led by Masoumeh Heidari Kapourchali (c15) will read temperature, acidity, salinity and oxygen (c14), say when a reactor's going to fail and what corrections could prevent it (c16, c17), and could quickly say a feedstock won't work instead of months if not years of trials (c34); NSF adds a virtual assay to screen feedstocks (c18). Briggs says it should speed the scale-up (c25).
counterpoint_to_honor: THE TEST, at full strength. Scale is where this field breaks. A DOE-funded pilot that pulled rare earths from coal material lost money on paper in every scenario (c22, a different, chemical-leach route, not UAA's), and for one feedstock its lab recovery ran about 30 percent higher than the pilot plant (c23). Reviews call bioleaching rare earths from waste still in its infancy (c24). And a neural network is usually limited by how much data it has (c26), while a new process starts with little, so the model may be weakest where it's needed most. Nothing is reported yet (c28). The film survives this by narrowing honestly: it claims the AI is aimed at the right wall, not that it gets over it.
who_it_serves: Alaskans weighing whether coal waste can be a critical-minerals asset (legislators, UA, economic development staff) who get a concrete test for 2030 (did the early no save trials, did recovery hold at scale); UAA and UAF researchers; anyone reading AI in a grant headline who wants to know what the model actually does.
second_movement: The reveal that recontextualises the hopeful open: UAA's own lab already did the hard-sounding part in the lab (c32) and stalled at scale (c33). So the grant is not a bet on new biology, it's a bet on a tool that says no faster. Then the test scene (c22, c23, c24, c26) and the turn: the four-or-five-step goal (c12) and the August 2030 end (c27) are the scoreboard.
